comments.body:
One really can't rely on GC to handle hardware resources - users in an environment that has a GC need to explicitly make sure they unmap resources instead of just letting them dangle. Someone familiar with the python bindings will need to see if whatever's happening inside there leaking mappings or something.

As for VMA, we'll be dropping our use at some point in the future and this limitation will go away. But it still won't be good practice and will have performance implications to keep the memory mapped even if you don't need it, and on some hardware it's not possible to launch new work on a device that has any host mappings active. This is just a reality of dealing with accelerator hardware.

I did a little digging in the Python API. The problem is that `iree.runtime.DeviceArray` holds the [mapping](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/ef6ef9019005488e42b1496c685d55dab263de66/runtime/bindings/python/iree/runtime/array_interop.py#L74) to the host array. 
I tried to make a function to clone the array list while relinquishing resources. I think this incurs an additional copy on the host side. I don't think there is a way around this with the current API.

```python
def clone_device_array_list_to_numpy(array_list: List[iree_rt.DeviceArray]) -> np.ndarray:
  res = [None]*len(array_list)
  while (len(array_list)):
    arr = array_list[-1].to_host() # this makes a copy.
    res[len(array_list) - 1] = np.copy(arr) # this also makes a copy.
    del array_list[-1]
  return res

iree_unet_optimizer_state = list(iree_module.get_unet_optimizer_state()) # this needs to be an editable collection. tuple is not.
iree_unet_optimizer_state = clone_device_array_list_to_numpy(iree_unet_optimizer_state)
```

On the compiler side. I think these arrays are put in a single allocation block. They are persistent across calls. In Python each one creates a mapping to the same allocation.

That'd probably do it! It's understandable at the python level here that having an array-like accessor makes this tricky as even if you map lazily on first access you don't know when to unmap. Ideally we'd only create the host mapping when needed for the shortest possible duration but with a single layer API (just DeviceArray) it's hard; this is why internally the runtime manages buffers (`iree_hal_buffer_t`) separately from the metadata wrapping them (`iree_hal_buffer_view_t`) and scopes all host mappings to the operations performing them. This is possible because there are no array accessor-like behaviors allowed - nothing touching accelerators is going to be good if you can't batch operations and reading individual elements out one at a time is a really sketchy thing to try to do in general (if you're reading device memory over a PCI bus you want to coalesce your reads/writes via big SIMD memcpys - round tripping one element at a time up through python could be hundreds of times slower as it could generate hundreds of times more PCI transactions).

Some workarounds for this may be to at least internally setup a buffer mapping on the python side: python device objects could internally have a dict of buffer pointers -> buffer wrappers and when a DeviceArray tried to map host memory it could go through that dict to see if it's already mapped instead of doing it locally. It still may run afoul of things (if the user allocated 256 unique buffers and mapped each one it'd still hit the limit) but harder in normal cases (users should allocate as few buffers as possible for inputs and arena/slab allocate instead of one buffer per input, and as you mention the compiler only ever returns a single slab buffer with all results).

Short-term solution would be to make VMA optional now that we have the caching allocator, but the caching allocator has lots of very sharp edges that make it suboptimal for anything but benchmarks/repeated invocations and currently VMA is our only proper suballocator. I've got some work I need to finish on our own suballocator before we can fully rip out VMA but don't have an ETA (could be a few days or a few weeks).

An even shorter term workaround would be to implement a `dispose` or something on the DeviceArray such that users could force them to be unmapped without waiting for GC. Eventually switching the mapping mode to `__enter__`/`__exit__` would be ideal for this kind of layer, letting you do things like:
```py
with device_array.contents() as c:  # map memory here in explicit scope
  print(c[0])  # access host bytes here
# host memory mapping released
```

But I leave the python stuff up to people who have a more pythonic mindset :)

You all do know that it is just code, right? :)

I'll need to grok this issue and attempt some surgery. Won't happen today but can get to it in the next 3.
I am not in a hurry for that one. I wanted to use the Vulkan backend as a reference to see what precision I get there.

issue.body:
### What happened?

I get this error when using a Vulkan module.
```
python: repo/third_party/vulkan_memory_allocator/include/vk_mem_alloc.h:12140: void VmaAllocation_T::BlockAllocMap(): Assertion `0 && "Allocation mapped too many times simultaneously."' failed.
```

It happens after when working with the returned arrays. I hit this rather low allocation mapping limit of 255. It seems to be related to the reference counting of the Python arrays.
I am not sure if this should be considered a bug. From a user's point of view I have a module that works in other backends and then fails in the Vulkan driver due to some peculiar limitation.


### Steps to reproduce your issue

1. Download and extract http://storage.googleapis.com/shark-public/boian/vulkan-alloc-mapped-too-many-times-data.tar.bz
2. Run this Python script in the same directory
```python
import iree.runtime
import numpy as np
from typing import List, TypeVar

Tensor = TypeVar('Tensor')


def array_equal(a: Tensor, b: Tensor):
    return np.array_equal(np.asarray(a), np.asarray(b))


def assert_array_list_compare(array_compare_fn, a: Tensor, b: Tensor):
    assert (len(a) == len(b))
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        np.testing.assert_array_compare(array_compare_fn, x, y)


def assert_array_list_equal(a: List[Tensor], b: List[Tensor]):
    assert_array_list_compare(array_equal, a, b)


jax_unet_optimizer_state = list(
    np.load("jax_unet_optimizer_state.npz").values())
iree_module = iree.runtime.system_api.load_vm_flatbuffer_file(
    "stable_diffusion_training_vulkan-spirv.vmfb", driver="vulkan")
assert_array_list_equal(iree_module.get_unet_optimizer_state(),
                        jax_unet_optimizer_state)

```


### What component(s) does this issue relate to?

Runtime
Python

### Version information

e5a8374bb198cbf8a73eb1a2b39d8b9d9ee973d8

### Additional context

I have also included the MLIR. It was compiled with
```
iree-compile \
  stable_diffusion_training.mlir \
  --iree-input-type=mhlo \
  --iree-vm-bytecode-module-output-format=flatbuffer-binary \
  --iree-hal-target-backends=vulkan-spirv \
  -o=stable_diffusion_training_vulkan-spirv.vmfb \
  --iree-llvm-embedded-linker-path=/home/petkantchin/ws/iree/build/ninja/RelWithDebInfo/compiler/bindings/python/iree/compiler/tools/../_mlir_libs/iree-lld' \
  --mlir-print-debuginfo \
  --mlir-print-op-on-diagnostic=false
```
issue.title: Vulkan driver: Allocation mapped too many times simultaneously
